Replication of genome‐wide association signals of type 2 diabetes in Han Chinese in a prospective cohort
Yi‐Cheng Chang, Yen‐Feng Chiu, Pi‐Hua Liu, Kuang‐Chung Shih, Ming‐Wei Lin, Wayne Huey‐Herng Sheu, Thomas Quertermous, Jess David Curb, Chano A. Hsiung, Wei‐Jei Lee, Po‐Chu Lee, Yuan‐Tsong Chen, Lee‐Ming Chuang

ABSTRACT
BACKGROUND: A recent genome-wide association study for type 2 diabetes in Han Chinese identified several novel genetic variants. We investigated their associations with quantitative measures to explore the mechanism by which these variants influence glucose homoeostasis. We also examined whether these variants predict progression to diabetes in a large prospective family based Chinese cohort. decisions.reason: Although the current source (Chang et al., 2011, 10.1111/j.1365-2265.2011.04175.x) supplies only the title and abstract without in-text citations (and full-text retrieval was unavailable), the new full primary XML of shipped row 226 (Tsai et al., 2010, PLoS Genetics, 10.1371/journal.pgen.1000847) establishes a unique descriptive bridge under Codebook Step 2 (identified_by = description). Chang et al. genotype five SNPs across four specific loci—PTPRD (rs17584499), SRR, MAF/WWOX (rs7192960), and KCNQ1 (rs2237897)—attributed to a recent Han Chinese type 2 diabetes GWAS. In Tsai et al. (2010), the two-stage Han Chinese discovery GWAS identifies novel genome-wide significant T2D associations at PTPRD (rs17584499, joint P = 8.54e-10) and SRR (rs391300, P = 3.06e-9; rs4523957, P = 1.44e-8), confirms KCNQ1 (rs2237892, rs2237895, rs2237897), and reports rs7192960 near MAF/WWOX in Table 1 as a suggestive Stage 1 signal (P = 7.66e-6) that failed Stage 2 replication (Stage 2 P = 0.037, joint P = 1.32e-5, not genome-wide significant). Other deposited East-Asian/Chinese diabetes references cover KCNQ1 or single components rather than this joint four-locus/SNP set. Beyond exploring glycemic mechanisms (HOMA-beta, HOMA-IR, OGTT insulin response), Chang et al. empirically retest the T2D risk association via prospective progression from nondiabetes to diabetes over 5.43 years in 1,138 Chinese participants (PTPRD rs17584499 TT hazard ratio = 8.82, P = 4e-5). Thus, target_index 0 is uniquely represented by shipped row 226; unseen full-text results are not assumed.

To remove or not to remove? Removal of the unconditional stimulus electrode does not mediate instructed extinction effects
Camilla C. Luck; Ottmar V. Lipp
10.1111/psyp.12452
Crossref abstract only
Abstract Following differential fear conditioning, the instruction that the unconditional stimulus will no longer be presented (instructed extinction) reduces differential electrodermal responding to CS+ and CS−, but does not affect differential conditional stimulus valence evaluations. Reductions in differential electrodermal responding have been attributed to the provision of verbal instructions; however, during instructed extinction the unconditional stimulus electrode is often removed as well. This removal could reduce the participants’ general arousal levels rendering the detection of differential electrodermal responding difficult. The current study examined this alternative interpretation by comparing the electrodermal responses and conditional stimulus valence evaluations of an instruction/electrode‐on group, an instruction/electrode‐off group, and a control group who were not instr
decisions.reason: The current source (Luck & Lipp, 2015, Psychophysiology, 10.1111/psyp.12452) is an abstract without in-text citations (full text unavailable), and fresh 0034 reference coding added no named citation. However, the newly supplied primary abstract of shipped row 1519 (Luck & Lipp, 2015, Behaviour Research and Therapy, 10.1016/j.brat.2015.01.001, present in the 26-entry deposited bibliography) establishes a unique compound protocol and finding bridge under Codebook Step 2 (identified_by = description). Shipped row 1519 specifically combined post-conditioning instructed extinction with removal of the shock electrode and tracked continuous self-reported conditional stimulus valence alongside physiological responding, finding that instructed extinction and shock-electrode removal immediately reduced differential fear-potentiated startle and electrodermal responding while conditional stimulus valence resisted instructed extinction. The current study directly tests whether that confounded US electrode removal mediated the physiological effect versus valence resistance by separating instruction/electrode-on, instruction/electrode-off, and non-instructed control groups, empirically retesting both endpoints and confirming that electrodermal responding was eliminated in both instructed groups whereas conditional stimulus valence was unaffected. Other deposited references address general evaluative conditioning, expectancy/affective learning, or emotional extinction expression rather than this compound instructed-extinction plus electrode-removal physiological-versus-valence dissociation. Modifying the design to unconfound electrode removal does not exclude conceptual/procedural retesting. Target_index 0 is therefore already represented by shipped row 1519, without asserting exhaustive knowledge of unseen full-text passages.

Reproducibility of effects of the homeopathic dilutions 14x - 30x of gibberellic acid on growth of Lemna gibba L.
Vera Majewsky; Claudia Scherr; Sebastian Arlt; Peter Klocke; Stephan Baumgartner

Background: Reproducibility of investigations in homeopathy is still challenging. Duckweed (Lemna gibba L.), a monocotyledonous waterplant which mostly reproduces vegetatively and therefore builds genetically identical clones, may be a suitable test system for standardised trials. Aims: This study investigated if formerly observed effects of gibberellic acid 14x – 30x on growth of Lemna gibba were reproducible. Methododology: Duckweed was grown in dilutions of gibberellic acid (14x–30x) as well as once succussed (c1) and unsuccussed (c0) water control. Area-related growth rate for day 0–7 was determined by a computerised image analysis system. Three series including five independent blinded and randomised experiments each were carried out in the same way as in the original study. Only time and conductor of experiments were modified. decisions.reason: The supplied text and recovered two-page publisher PDF (Majewsky, Scherr, Arlt, Klocke, & Baumgartner, 2012, Int J High Dilution Res 11(40):196-197, 10.51910/ijhdr.v11i40.598) constitute the complete published proceedings report, which contains no in-text citation or reference list. The newly supplied primary abstract of shipped row 965 (Scherr, Simon, Spranger, & Baumgartner, 2009, Complementary Therapies in Medicine 17(2):63-70, 10.1016/j.ctim.2008.10.004) establishes a unique compound method and finding fingerprint under Codebook Step 2 (identified_by = description). Scherr et al. (2009) grew Lemna gibba L. for 7 days in decimal potencies 14x-30x versus unsuccussed and succussed water controls, measured frond area-related growth rate r(area) for day 0-7 via computerised image analysis across series of five to six independent randomized, blinded experiments per substance alongside repeated systematic negative control (SNC) water experiments, and evaluated global F-tests followed by protected Fisher's LSD tests. Among four substances screened in Scherr et al. (2009) (gibberellic acid, kinetin, argentum nitricum, Lemna minor), gibberellic acid 14x-30x yielded the most pronounced effect (p = 0.0002) and decreased r(area) day 0-7 (protected LSD p < 0.05). Majewsky et al. (2012) isolate that exact gibberellic acid 14x-30x arm and repeat three five-experiment blinded, randomized series plus three five-experiment SNC series ('carried out in the same way as in the original study. Only time and conductor of experiments were modified'), explicitly contrasting their third-series growth increase with 'decreasing in the former study.' Target_index 0 is uniquely represented by shipped row 965.

## Abstract
### Objectives:

Mental health concerns on university campuses are increasing in the UK. Improving mental health literacy (MHL) for students may be a useful part of an integrated approach to effectively address these concerns. This study evaluated a previously demonstrated effective Canadian campus MHL resource in a UK student sample.
### Design:

This cross-sectional study conducted on one UK campus reports on student’s opinions about the impact of the Transitions (2nd edition) resource as well as applying a standard measure of MHL.

### Methods:

Online survey using a convenience sample of students during semester 1 conducted over a 1-week period at a large UK university.

decisions.reason: The current source (Hunt, Wei, & Kutcher, 2019, Health Education Journal, 10.1177/0017896919826374) supplies the title, abstract, and unnumbered reference list, while the full article body remains unavailable. The newly supplied primary abstracts for all three cited Canadian postsecondary Transitions evaluation studies (remaining_identity_sources_0170) resolve the prior ambiguity under Codebook Step 2 (identified_by = description). Hunt et al. (2019) conduct a cross-sectional online survey at one UK university reporting students' opinions about the impact of reading the Transitions (2nd edition) resource and a standard MHL measure, finding improved mental health knowledge, decreased stigma, and increased help-seeking intent. Shipped row 112 (Kutcher, Wei, & Morgan, 2016c, Health Education Journal 75:689-697, 10.1177/0017896915610144) is the exact Canadian counterpart evaluating standalone reading of Transitions (2nd edition) at a single large Canadian university via a survey of students' opinions of the resource's impact, reporting the same triad of improved mental health knowledge, decreased stigma, and enhanced help-seeking efficacy/intentions. By contrast, Potvin-Boucher et al. (2010) evaluated the 2007 launch of the 1st edition (reporting only that >95% related to/enjoyed it and 40% discussed it with a friend, with the newly surfaced archive lead returning restricted HTML rather than a report body), and Gilham et al. (2018) evaluated peer-led seminars across three training/participant groups rather than standalone booklet reading and student opinion ratings. Thus, the compound resource-edition, delivery, and three-outcome fingerprint uniquely identifies shipped row 112, without assuming unseen full-text results.
